title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
Udio, an AI music generation service, trained its models on recorded music without obtaining licenses from the rights holders. The core failure is a system built on data it had no authorization to use, a problem that originates in the training pipeline rather than in the model's runtime behavior. Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group each settled their lawsuits and entered licensing arrangements with Udio, while Sony Music filed a separate new lawsuit alleging that approximately 30,000 of its recordings were used without permission. A class action brought by independent artists was also allowed to proceed, transferred from Illinois to New York rather than dismissed.

This is an unauthorized training-data failure. Catching it would have required rights clearance before ingestion, the kind of legal review that sits outside the model development process itself and must be imposed as a condition of data selection. There is no indication that any such clearance process was in place when the training corpus was assembled.

What is not established: the lawsuits are allegations, not adjudicated findings, and no court has issued a ruling that Udio infringed any copyright. The settlements with UMG and WMG resolved their claims without any public admission of liability, and Sony's new lawsuit remains in early litigation.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which had been accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. The companies reached licensing agreements, and Udio will launch a new platform next year that uses only authorized and licensed music. Under the agreement, artists can opt into the platform and will receive compensation, though specific financial terms and participating artists were not disclosed. UMG's chairman emphasized the settlement demonstrates the company's commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies and developing fresh business models.

The original lawsuit alleged that Udio had improperly trained its AI on copyrighted recordings, including hits like The Temptations' "My Girl," to create similar compositions without permission or payment. This marks the first major music licensing agreement Udio has secured with a major record label. The company, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, has attracted millions of users since launching its app and website.
